order.subject: math
order.topic: Multi-step word problems with multiplication and division (remainders)
order.requests: Real-world stories, please (our farm stand, the co-op, trips). Level 3 needs two steps. In each level, put one problem where the remainder changes the answer: round up, drop it, or the remainder is the answer.

itemRequests.worksheet: About 12 problems, easiest first. Leave room to show work.
itemRequests.quiz: 10 questions. Version B should be just as hard as A.

notes: Name and Date on one line in a box; bold directions that start with "Your job:"
Questions numbered 1) with a closing parenthesis; choices as (A) (B) (C) (D)
Short, friendly stories from the farm stand, co-op, library, garden and trips
Answer blanks carry the unit; students show their thinking
Parts go Warm-Up, On Your Own, Two-Step Challenge ★; star problems have a "Think:" planning line
Key: each answer on its own line, the answer, a dash, then the short calculation; remainders and estimates noted

documents.title: Farm Stand and Co-op: Remainders in Stories (Week 9)
documents.directions: Your job: Read each story twice. Show your thinking in the space. Picture the last group: does the leftover still need a place? Write your answer with its unit.

questions.prompt: The farm stand has 7 crates of corn. Each crate holds 24 ears of corn. How many ears of corn is that? Think: 7 groups of 24.
29 kids are going to the pumpkin patch. Each car holds 4 kids. How many cars do we need so every kid gets a ride? Hint: 29 ÷ 4 = 7 R1. Does the leftover kid still need a car?
questions.why: 8 cars — 29 ÷ 4 = 7 R1; round up, the 1 kid left still needs a car

questions.prompt: Our hens laid 45 eggs. We sell eggs in cartons of 6. How many full cartons can we sell? Hint: 45 ÷ 6 = 7 R3. Can 3 eggs fill a carton?
questions.why: 7 cartons — 45 ÷ 6 = 7 R3; drop the 3, they can't fill a carton

questions.prompt: The library gives 39 bookmarks to 5 kids to share equally. How many bookmarks are left over? Hint: 39 ÷ 5 = 7 R4. What is the question asking about?
questions.why: 4 bookmarks — 39 ÷ 5 = 7 R4; the question asks what is left, so the remainder is the answer

questions.prompt: The co-op garden has 23 rows of carrots. There are 18 carrots in each row. How many carrots are in the garden?
52 people are going on the co-op trip to the science museum. Each van holds 8 people. How many vans do we need so everyone can go?
questions.why: 7 vans — 52 ÷ 8 = 6 R4; round up, the 4 people left still need a seat

questions.prompt: Mom baked 158 muffins for the farm stand. She puts 6 muffins in each box. How many full boxes can she sell?
questions.why: 26 boxes — 158 ÷ 6 = 26 R2; drop the 2, they can't make a full box

questions.prompt: The library has 250 stickers. 7 classes share them equally. How many stickers are left over?
questions.why: 5 stickers — 250 ÷ 7 = 35 R5; the question asks what is left, so the answer is the remainder

questions.skill: two steps: times as many, then add
questions.prompt: On Friday the farm stand sold 145 ears of corn. On Saturday it sold 3 times as many. How many ears of corn did it sell on both days? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.

questions.skill: two steps: multiply, then divide (drop it)
questions.prompt: The garden club picked 6 buckets of 47 tomatoes. They put 8 tomatoes in each bag to sell. How many full bags can they sell? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
questions.why: 35 bags — 6 × 47 = 282, then 282 ÷ 8 = 35 R2; drop the 2; estimate: 6 × 50 = 300, 300 ÷ 8 is about 37, close to 35

questions.skill: two steps: divide (round up), then multiply
questions.prompt: 75 people are coming to the co-op harvest supper. Each table seats 6. We set up enough tables so everyone has a seat. Each table gets a jar with 3 sunflowers. How many sunflowers do we need? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
questions.why: 39 sunflowers — 75 ÷ 6 = 12 R3, round up to 13 tables (the 3 people still need a seat), then 13 × 3 = 39; estimate: 75 is close to 72, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 tables, plus 1 for the leftover people is about 13, and 13 × 3 is about 40, close to 39

questions.skill: two steps: multiply, then divide (remainder is the answer)
questions.prompt: The library got 4 boxes of 65 new books. They put 9 books on each cart and fill as many carts as they can. How many books are left over? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
questions.why: 8 books — 4 × 65 = 260, then 260 ÷ 9 = 28 R8; the answer is the remainder; check: 9 × 28 = 252, 252 + 8 = 260; estimate: 270 ÷ 9 = 30 carts, so about 28 carts makes sense

documents.title: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9)
documents.directions: Your job: Read each story twice. Show your thinking. Circle the letter or write the answer with its unit.

prompt.A: The co-op orders 6 cases of jam. Each case has 24 jars. How many jars is that?
prompt.B: The garden has 7 rows of beans. Each row has 32 bean plants. How many bean plants is that?

prompt.A: The co-op has 96 seed packets. 8 families share them equally. Let p be the number of packets each family gets. Which equation fits the story?
prompt.B: The farm stand has 84 jars of jam. Dad puts them on 7 shelves, the same number on each. Let j be the number of jars on each shelf. Which equation fits the story?

why.A: (B) 96 ÷ 8 = p — sharing equally is dividing: 96 packets ÷ 8 families
why.B: (C) 84 ÷ 7 = j — putting the same number on each shelf is dividing: 84 jars ÷ 7 shelves

prompt.A: 34 kids are going to the library story day. Each car holds 4 kids. How many cars do we need so every kid gets a ride? Picture the last group.
prompt.B: 57 people are coming to the co-op picnic. Each table seats 6. How many tables do we need so everyone has a seat? Picture the last group.

why.A: 9 cars — 34 ÷ 4 = 8 R2; round up, the 2 kids left still need a car
why.B: 10 tables — 57 ÷ 6 = 9 R3; round up, the 3 people left still need a seat

prompt.A: Our hens laid 125 eggs this week. We sell eggs in cartons of 6. How many full cartons can we sell?
prompt.B: Mom baked 142 muffins. She puts 4 muffins in each box. How many full boxes can she sell at the farm stand?

why.A: 20 cartons — 125 ÷ 6 = 20 R5; drop the 5, they can't fill a carton
why.B: 35 boxes — 142 ÷ 4 = 35 R2; drop the 2, they can't fill a box

prompt.A: 47 kids from the co-op are going canoeing. Each canoe holds 3 kids. 47 ÷ 3 = 15 R2. How many canoes do we need so every kid can go?
prompt.B: The farm stand has 82 eggs. Eggs go in cartons of 6. 82 ÷ 6 = 13 R4. How many full cartons can we sell?

why.A: (D) 16 canoes — round up, the 2 kids left still need a canoe
why.B: (A) 13 cartons — drop the 4, they can't fill a carton

prompt.A: The library has 200 bookmarks. 6 classes share them equally. How many bookmarks are left over?
prompt.B: The garden club has 150 bean seeds. 8 kids share them equally. How many seeds are left over?

why.A: 2 bookmarks — 200 ÷ 6 = 33 R2; the question asks what is left, so the answer is the remainder
why.B: 6 seeds — 150 ÷ 8 = 18 R6; the question asks what is left, so the answer is the remainder

questions.skill: two steps: multiply, then divide (drop it)

prompt.A: The farm stand picked 5 crates of 38 apples. We put 6 apples in each bag. How many full bags can we sell? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
prompt.B: The garden grew 6 rows of 43 carrots. Dad ties 8 carrots in each bunch. How many full bunches can he sell? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.

why.A: 31 bags — 5 × 38 = 190, then 190 ÷ 6 = 31 R4; drop the 4; estimate: 5 × 40 = 200, 200 ÷ 6 is about 33, close to 31
why.B: 32 bunches — 6 × 43 = 258, then 258 ÷ 8 = 32 R2; drop the 2; estimate: 6 × 40 = 240, 240 ÷ 8 = 30, close to 32

questions.skill: two steps: divide (round up), then multiply

prompt.A: 58 people are going on the co-op trip to the apple orchard. Each van holds 8 people. Each van costs $40 for the day. What will the vans cost in all? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
prompt.B: 45 kids are going to the county fair. Each car holds 4 kids. Gas for each car costs $9. What will the gas cost in all? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.

why.A: (C) $320 — 58 ÷ 8 = 7 R2, round up to 8 vans, then 8 × $40 = $320; check: 7 × 8 = 56 is just under 58, so 7 vans are not enough; estimate: 58 is about 60 people, 60 ÷ 8 is about 8 vans, 8 × $40 = $320
why.B: (B) $108 — 45 ÷ 4 = 11 R1, round up to 12 cars, then 12 × $9 = $108; estimate: 12 × 10 = 120, close to 108

questions.skill: two steps: multiply, then divide (remainder is the answer)

prompt.A: The library got 3 boxes of 85 new books. They put 9 books in each crate for the school visit and fill as many crates as they can. How many books are left over? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.
prompt.B: The garden club has 4 packs of 75 seeds. They plant 7 seeds in each pot and fill as many pots as they can. How many seeds are left over? Think: What do I find first? Then estimate to check.

why.A: 3 books — 3 × 85 = 255, then 255 ÷ 9 = 28 R3; the answer is the remainder; check: 9 × 28 = 252, 252 + 3 = 255; estimate: 3 × 90 = 270, 270 ÷ 9 = 30 crates, so about 28 makes sense
why.B: 6 seeds — 4 × 75 = 300, then 300 ÷ 7 = 42 R6; the answer is the remainder; check: 7 × 42 = 294, 294 + 6 = 300; estimate: 280 ÷ 7 = 40 pots, so about 42 makes sense

notes: Round 1: Style agent read 2 examples and wrote 33 style notes. Maker wrote 12 worksheet problems (4 per level, every level with round-up, drop-it and remainder-is-the-answer stories) and quiz A/B (10 each: 4 mc, 6 typed, L1 3, L2 4, L3 3). Before hand-off the maker's self-check caught one converge-bot fail at 53% vs 25% chance; the maker fixed wrong choices in q2 both versions, q5 B, q7 both versions, and A q9, and the bots then passed.

Round 1 Wilco: keys check passed (32 rows, 0 errors). Test-wise bots passed on the 8 quiz choice questions (chance 25%; worst was largest 50%, round 37.5%, middle 31.3%). The pack has only 2 all-number choice questions (q9 A and B), below the 3 needed to judge the largest-number cue, so it was shown but not judged. Most items are typed answers which the bots don't play.
Round 1 blind tester: solved all 32 items from the student copy with no key, matched 32 of 32. Then read the key and decided 6 FIX, 2 JUDGMENT for the teacher, 1 KEEP.

FIX A q7 and B q7: two wrong choices in each had remainders bigger than the divisor (A: 56 R11 and 50 R47; B: 74 R11 and 70 R39) and multiplied back to the dividend, leaving test-wise students with a 50/50. Fixed round 2: all wrong choices now have remainders under the divisor and none rebuild to the dividend.

FIX w11: story said 'we set up' tables but never said everyone must be seated, so a student could defend 12 full tables. Fixed round 2: added 'enough tables so everyone has a seat' so rounding up is the only reading.
FIX w4: opening sentence put the 5 kids before the 39 bookmarks and read clumsily. Fixed round 2: reworded to 'The library gives 39 bookmarks to 5 kids to share equally.'

FIX A q9 why: estimate step was 8 × 40 = 320, the exact calculation, not a real estimate. Fixed round 2: estimate now rounds 58 to about 60, so 60 ÷ 8 is about 8 vans and 8 × $40 = $320, plus a check that 7 vans are too few.

KEEP quiz Level 3 share (raised as FIX by blind tester): each version has 10 items with only 3 Level 3 (30%), below the 40% target. Order lead decision: the 40% rule is for unit tests; the menu quiz has no Level 3 share, and the teacher asked only that Level 3 need two steps, which all three do in both versions.
KEEP w9: it's a two-step problem with no remainder. The notes review 'times as many' this week, and w10–w12 cover all three remainder types at Level 3.

JUDGMENT for teacher q5 A/B: A rounds up (canoes) and B drops the remainder (full cartons), so the two versions test different remainder moves at the same spot. Both are fair Level 2 items with the division given, and each version covers all three remainder types.

JUDGMENT for teacher A q9 choices: B q9 has a multiply-everything trap ($405 = 45 × 9) but A has none. The matching A trap would be 58 × $40 = $2,320. Both versions already have the dropped-remainder trap ($280 and $99).

Round 1 solver: worked all 32 answers on its own with node scripts, every step: 0 disagreements. Found 2 JUDGMENT (q7 choices that multiply back, same as blind's finding; B q10 friendlier first step with 4 × 75 = 300 vs A's 3 × 85 = 255) and 2 KEEP (B q5 key shown in prompt, intentional; w12 estimate uses compatible numbers).

Round 2 recheck: blind tester solved the 5 changed items, matched 5 of 5, confirmed all 5 round 2 fixes. Found 1 new FIX in teacher copy: w11's estimate started from the exact 13 tables instead of rounding, the same flaw fixed on A q9. Wilco passed (0 errors, same worst bots).

Round 3: maker rewrote w11's teacher estimate to round first (75 ≈ 72, 72 ÷ 6 = 12, plus 1 ≈ 13, 13 × 3 ≈ 40). Wilco passed. Recheck solved w11 blind (39, matched), confirmed the fix, found nothing new.

Preview check by the order lead: the worksheet and quiz printed each typed question's answer blank twice (the maker had written 'Answer: ____ <unit>' into 24 prompts, and the page adds its own Answer line). The inline blanks were removed; the directions still ask for the unit. Nothing else changed.

Three judgment calls wait for the teacher: quiz q5 (A rounds up, B drops the remainder), A q9 (no 'multiply the two numbers' wrong choice like B q9's $405), and B q10 (its first step, 4 × 75 = 300, is friendlier than A's 3 × 85 = 255).

How to read Wilco's charts: the 'keys' rounds have no chance line (they check keys, not guessing), and the 'largest' bar at 50% is drawn over the line but was not judged: it needs 3 all-number choice questions and this pack has 2 (A q9's key is the largest choice, B q9's is not).

Totals: wall clock 18 minutes (14:13 to 14:31 UTC, first to last agent row). Agent minutes 14.6: style notes 0.7, maker 5.0 over 3 rounds (4.3 + 0.5 + 0.2), blind testers 4.8 over 3 rounds, solver 1.8, reporter 2.3. Tokens 4,013,808 and cost $5.48, both exact as each session reported them (its own dollars, at list API prices); most tokens are cache reads of the briefs and the pack. Wilco's scripts and the order lead's steps use no model tokens and are not measured. Per question: 32 question rows (12 worksheet, 10 in each quiz version), about $0.17 each.

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q7
findings.what: Two wrong choices (B 56 R11, D 50 R47) are true number sentences (6×56+11 and 6×50+47 both make 347) with remainders bigger than the divisor. A student who checks by multiplying finds three choices that work, and a test-wise student crosses out both and is left with a 50/50 against C. Key A is right. Change B to 56 R5 and D to 57 R1: each remainder is under 6 and each is wrong. Optional: give it a short story so it fits the word-problem quiz.
findings.fixed: Wrong choices now 59 R3, 58 R1, 51 R1: none multiplies back to 347 and every remainder is under 6; key A (57 R5) stays. (confirmed by the round 2 recheck)

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) B q7
findings.what: Same flaw as A q7: choices A (74 R11) and C (70 R39) multiply back to 529 but have remainders of 7 or more, so a test-wise student can drop them. Key D is right. Change A to 74 R4 and C to 75 R6: each remainder is under 7 and each is wrong.
findings.fixed: Wrong choices now 71 R2, 76 R3, 74 R1: none multiplies back to 529 and every remainder is under 7; key D (75 R4) stays. (confirmed by the round 2 recheck)

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q8
findings.what: Raised as FIX by the blind tester: Quiz balance: each version has 10 items and only 3 are Level 3 (q8–q10), which is 30% against the brief's target of about 40%. Turn one Level 2 item into a two-step Level 3 story. q7, the bare division item, is the natural one to change (for example a multiply-then-divide story with a remainder), in both A and B. That also fixes the q7 test-wise problem.
findings.reason: Order lead decision, not sent to the maker: the about-40% Level 3 rule is for unit tests (maker.md rule 3, checks/keys.mjs); the menu quiz has no Level 3 share, and the teacher asked only that Level 3 need two steps, which all three do in both versions.

findings.where: Farm Stand and Co-op: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) w11
findings.what: The why says the leftover 3 people still need a seat, but the story never says everyone must be seated at a table. A student could defend 12 full tables × 3 = 36. Add a few words such as 'We set up enough tables so everyone has a seat' so that rounding up is the only reading. Key 39 stays.
findings.fixed: Added 'enough tables so everyone has a seat', so rounding up to 13 tables is the only reading; key 39 stays. (confirmed by the round 2 recheck)

findings.where: Farm Stand and Co-op: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) w4
findings.what: The opening sentence puts the 5 kids before the 39 bookmarks and reads clumsily. Reword it to 'The library gives 39 bookmarks to 5 kids to share equally.' Key 4 stays.
findings.fixed: Opening reworded to put the 39 bookmarks first; reads cleanly; key 4 stays. (confirmed by the round 2 recheck)

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q9
findings.what: The why line's estimate step (8 × 40 = 320) is just the exact calculation again, so it shows no real estimating. The teacher's notes want a real estimate check on Level 3, for example 58 is about 60 people, 60 ÷ 8 is about 8 vans, and 8 × $40 = $320. Key C is right.
findings.fixed: The why's estimate now rounds 58 to about 60, so 60 ÷ 8 is about 8 vans and 8 × $40 = $320 (a real estimate); it also adds a check that 7 × 8 = 56 is too few. Key C stays. (confirmed by the round 2 recheck)

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q9
findings.what: Choices don't match across versions: B q9 has a 'multiply the two numbers you see' wrong choice ($405 = 45 × 9), but A has none. The matching A choice would be 58 × $40 = $2,320. Reading 1: add $2,320 in place of $48 so the trap is the same in A and B. Reading 2: leave it, since both versions already have the dropped-remainder trap ($280 and $99), which is the one that matters.
findings.reason: Not changed by the agents: left for the teacher to decide in the preview (REVIEW.html), as the runbook says for a judgment call.

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q5
findings.what: A asks students to round up (canoes) and B asks them to drop the remainder (full cartons). Both are fair Level 2 items with the division given, but the two versions test different remainder moves at the same spot. Reading 1: keep, because round-up is no harder than drop-it and each version still covers all three remainder types somewhere. Reading 2: make B a round-up story so the pair matches item for item.
findings.reason: Not changed by the agents: left for the teacher to decide in the preview (REVIEW.html), as the runbook says for a judgment call.

findings.where: Farm Stand and Co-op: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) w9
findings.what: It's a real two-step problem ('times as many', then 'both days') with no remainder. That's fine: the notes review 'times as many' this week, and w10–w12 cover all three remainder types at Level 3.

findings.where: Farm Stand and Co-op: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) w11
findings.what: Teacher copy only: the why's estimate ('about 13 tables × 3 is about 40') starts from the exact 13 tables, so it repeats the calculation instead of estimating. This is the same flaw round 1 fixed on A q9. Use a real rounding instead, e.g. 75 is close to 72, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 tables plus 1 for the leftover people is 13, and 13 × 3 is about 40. Key 39 and the student copy stay.
findings.fixed: The why's estimate now rounds 75 to 72 first (72 ÷ 6 = 12, plus 1 for leftover = about 13), then estimates 13 × 3 ≈ 40. This is a real estimate check, not a repetition of the exact calculation. The round 2 finding is fixed. (confirmed by the round 3 recheck)

findings.where: Co-op Quiz: Remainders in Stories (Week 9) A q7
